newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe cuts taxes in new tariff regime.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe cuts taxes in new tariff regime.

text.p: Zimbabwe scrapped import duty on capital goods on Friday and announced deep cuts in tax on industrial spares in a new tariff regime it said was aimed at boosting its sickly manufacturing and industrial sectors.
Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa told a news conference that the long-awaited tariff cuts, which were heartily welcomed by commerce and industry, would take effect from March 1.
But he said the new taxes would not apply in areas where the southern African country has preferential trading pacts, including South Africa with which it is negotiating a crucial economic agreement.

Duties on raw materials for manufacturing and on books have been slashed to five percent from 40 percent; on spares to 15 percent from up to 56 percent and on partly processed inputs to 15 percent from up to 55 percent.

Import tax on capital goods was cut to zero from a 0-25 percent pegging and also to zero from 10 percent on goods for the blind, although the government retained a 20 percent import duty on other medical supllies.
Murerwa said finished imported goods would attract duty of between 40 to 85 percent from 0-85 percent, with the highest tariffs applying to electronics, batteries, luggageware, textile and clothing.

Zimbabwe has signed an agreement in principle with South Africa requiring Pretoria to restore to about 30 percent duty on Zimbabwean textile and clothing exports, which it trippled in 1992 saying it wanted to protect its own industry.

The South African move crippled Zimbabwe's industry, and the latter has since been accusing its neighbour and main trading partner on the continent of trying to sabotage its economy by dumping goods on its market at subsidised rates.
Pretoria vehemently denies the charges, and is locked in lengthy talks over a new trade agreement with Harare.

"This (tariff regime) is not aimed at retaliating against any one of our trading partners. They are part of our economic reforms to boost manufacturing, industrial growth and general economic growth and development," Murerwa told a news conference.
Asked whether the new duties would affect Zimbabwe's trade talks with South Africa or the two's agreement in principle on textiles and clothing, he said: "No, they should not".
Joe Foroma, the chief executive of the Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries (CZI), said the new tariffs were on the face of it welcome and should help boost economic growth.
"We have been waiting for them for a long time...but we can only make a comprehensive assessment after studying the tariffs in detail," he said of the 1,500-page document.
The Zimbabwe government announced a new tariff regime last August, but withdrew it after a week under pressure from industrialists who said they had not been consulted.
"I am confident and hopeful that this will be accepted by everyone because we consulted extensively and took on board a large part of the recommendations we got from industry," Murerwa said.

Ministry of finance officials said the tariffs had been structured in such a way that there would be no loss or gain in government revenue from expected import duty this year. -- Harare Newsroom: +263-4 72 52 27/8/9
